name: Orbital shapes: 1s through 3d
description: A walking tour through the distinctive geometries of s, p, and d orbitals, all rendered on the same element (argon) so only the quantum numbers change.

steps.caption: 1s — the simplest orbital. A single solid sphere of probability density centred on the nucleus, with no nodes anywhere. Every atom's innermost electrons live here.
2s — still spherical, but now with a radial node. Look for the thin gap separating a dense inner ball from a fluffier outer shell. Same shape family as 1s, one principal-quantum-number step up.
2p_z — first non-spherical shape. Same n as 2s, but l jumped from 0 to 1, producing the famous dumbbell aligned along the z axis. The plane through the nucleus is an angular node.
3s — back to a sphere, now with two radial nodes. Nested onion shells of density: count the gaps and you've counted (n − l − 1) radial nodes.
3p_z — the dumbbell returns, but each lobe is now split by a radial node. Same angular shape as 2p_z, just one extra ring of nodal structure baked in.
3d_z² — a stranger beast. Two big lobes along z plus a doughnut-shaped ring around the equator. This is what bumping l from 1 to 2 buys you: richer angular structure.
3d_xy — the classic cloverleaf. Four lobes hanging between the x and y axes. Same (n, l) as the previous step; only m changed, rotating the angular pattern into a different geometric flavour.
